This page is written according to U.S. O*NET-SOC 11-9071.00 “Gambling Managers” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese name for Gambling Managers; the main objects are gambling operations and house rules and pricing and personnel and compliance and anti-money laundering controls in a licensed casino, and the output is compliantly operated venue and game and fund and licensing results). Important jurisdictional boundary: this page describes legal positions in jurisdictions such as the United States that allow licensed gambling; in mainland China, apart from the state-approved lotteries issued in accordance with the law, gambling and operating casinos are strictly prohibited by the Criminal Law and other laws, and this legal U.S. position cannot be treated as an occupation path that can be operated in mainland China; before getting involved, the law and authorization of the location must first be verified.

Editorial exploration｜M/V2 anonymized paper verifies eligibility and scheduling, independent fund balances, actual expenses paid, and complaint status; the deliverables only observe recalculation, authority, and traceability, and do not confer real manager qualifications.

Fit signals｜O*NET focus points: continuous contact with others (79% continuous contact), daily face-to-face discussions (93% every day), daily decisions affecting others and organizational resources (86% every day), working with a work group or team extremely important (81%), coordinating or leading others extremely important (77%), must be very precise or highly accurate “extremely important” (62%) and “very important” (28%), freedom to make decisions without supervision “a lot” (51%) and “some” (33%), daily email use (69%) and daily telephone use (57%), and “very high” responsibility for others' health and safety (53%). If you are willing to take on both business decisions and personnel and compliance responsibility in a highly regulated venue and to keep judgment and records consistent amid high-frequency communication, this occupation's daily demands are closer to your working style.

Caution signals｜O*NET also shows: consequences of error “extremely serious” (29%) and “very serious” (31%) and “serious” (18%), with “not at all serious” only 13%; need to deal with unpleasant or angry or impolite people every day (26% every day, 49% at least weekly but not daily); competition level “extremely competitive” (21%) and “highly competitive” (26%); daily time pressure from strict deadlines (34% every day, 31% at least weekly but not daily); work week exceeding 40 hours (47%); physical proximity “moderately close (within arm's reach)” (59%) and “very close” (18%); continuous or almost continuous standing (28%) and standing about half the time (33%), continuous or almost continuous sitting (22%) and less than half (37%); public speaking every day (20%). This occupation centers on venue operations and pricing and personnel and compliance and anti-money laundering controls: one mishandled pricing or credit or payout dispute, one case of cheating or anomalies and suspicious activity not identified and reported, or one failure in scheduling or funds or records or compliance can cause licensing and fines and reputational and financial consequences; moreover, gambling is strictly restricted by law in mainland China, and before getting involved the law and authorization of the location must be verified, and if you find it hard to bear decision consequences and compliance pressure over the long term in a highly regulated and responsibility-concentrated management environment, these should be treated as real costs requiring careful weighing.

Independently complete the four M/V2 deliverables and three counterexamples; no real venue funds or senior sign-off are needed, and real experience, training, registration, and management appointment are verified separately.

The three types of task focus may cross over: business rules and game knowledge and marketing, personnel patrol and customers, and funds and compliance records; the source tasks are not a uniform division of labor for everyone.

O*NET occupational profile highlights｜The official scope of O*NET-SOC 11-9071.00 “Gambling Managers” is: Plan, direct, or coordinate gambling operations in a casino. May formulate house rules. Of the 20 tasks given in the occupational profile, 12 are core tasks: handle customer complaints such as payout errors; eject suspected cheaters (such as card counters or others who may possess systems that change the odds); track fund replenishment for each table and handle the required paperwork; answer and explain house rules (such as game rules or wagering limits); schedule work sheets and station assignments and keep attendance; monitor staffing levels to ensure adequate game and table personnel for each shift, arrange employee rotations and breaks and find substitutes as needed; be familiar with all games in the venue and the strategies or tricks used in those games; train new employees or evaluate their performance; market or promote the casino to attract business; interview and hire employees; direct the granting of room and meal comps or other discounts or complimentary items based on player playing time and total wagering; and formulate policies on possible issues (such as the gambling types offered and the odds, credit granting, and food and beverage service). There are another 7 supplemental tasks: patrol between tables to ensure operations are conducted according to the rules, dealers follow house rules, and players are not cheating; set and maintain a fund pool and table limits for each game; direct the preparation of summary sheets showing wager amounts and payouts for each match or event; review the accuracy of operating expenses and budget estimates and wagering accounts or collection reports; record and collect or pay out wagers and issue receipts as needed; notify ushers of open tables so waiting players can be seated; monitor the credit extended to players. There is another 1 new task: monitor the operating performance of the gambling hall and move games and install new games when needed.

entries: Business rules and game knowledge and marketing｜Policy and promotion｜Formulate game type, odds, credit, and food and beverage policies within actual authorization, be familiar with in-house games and strategies, and market and promote the casino; this is not profitable instruction.

Limits and hall｜Fund pool and game layout｜Set and maintain a fund pool and table limits for each game, track fund replenishment for each table and handle the required paperwork, and monitor the operating performance of the gambling hall and move games and install new games when needed.

Personnel and training｜Scheduling and hiring and performance｜Schedule work sheets and station assignments and keep attendance, monitor staffing levels by shift and arrange rotations and breaks and substitutes, and interview and hire employees, train new employees, and evaluate their performance.

Patrol and order｜Anti-cheating and complimentary items｜Patrol between tables to ensure operations are conducted according to the rules and that dealers follow house rules and players are not cheating, eject suspected cheaters (such as card counters), decide the granting of complimentary items based on playing time and total wagering, and notify ushers of open tables.

Funds and bookkeeping｜Wagering and credit and review｜Record and collect or pay out wagers and issue receipts as needed, monitor the credit extended to players, direct the preparation of wagering and payout summary sheets, and review operating expenses and budget estimates and wagering accounts and collection reports.

Customers and compliance｜Complaints and licensing and anti-money laundering｜Handle customer complaints such as payout errors, answer and explain house rules, implement licensing and registration and anti-money laundering and customer identification and age limit requirements, and identify and report anomalies and suspicious activity.

Jurisdictional, compliance, and data boundaries｜This page involves three types of requirements: first, jurisdiction — in jurisdictions such as the United States, gambling must be operated lawfully within licensed venues and approved channels and comply with jurisdictional rules and gambling operations and credit and record requirements, while in mainland China, apart from lotteries issued under legal approval, gambling and operating casinos are strictly prohibited by the Criminal Law and other laws, and the legal U.S. position on this page cannot serve as an occupation path that can be operated in mainland China; second, anti-money laundering and customer identification and age limits — licensed venues must implement customer identification and transaction records and suspicious activity identification and staff training and escalation mechanisms (such as the U.S. FinCEN recordkeeping and reporting and compliance program requirements for casinos), and managers must not weaken these controls on their own, nor permit service to minors or self-excluded or restricted persons; third, information and records — customer and employee identity and transaction and wagering data must be limited to authorized and compliance purposes and managed on a minimum-necessary basis with retention periods. This page provides general prompts only and does not constitute legal or compliance or investment advice.

subject.name: Gambling Managers
subject.summary: Gambling Managers (O*NET-SOC 11-9071.00, Gambling Managers) plan, direct, or coordinate gambling operations in a licensed casino and may be responsible for formulating house rules: establish policies such as which gambling types are offered and the odds and credit granting and food and beverage service; set and maintain a fund pool and table limits for each game; track fund replenishment for each table and handle the required paperwork; monitor the operating performance of the gambling hall and move games when needed and install new games; schedule work sheets and station assignments and keep attendance; monitor staffing levels by shift and arrange rotations and breaks and substitutes as needed; interview and hire employees, train new employees, and evaluate their performance; patrol between tables to ensure operations are conducted according to the rules and that dealers follow house rules and players are not cheating, and eject suspected cheaters (such as card counters); decide the granting of compliments such as room and meal comps and discounts based on player playing time and total wagering; notify ushers of open tables so waiting players can be seated; handle customer complaints such as payout errors; answer and explain house rules (game rules or wagering limits); record and collect or pay out wagers and issue receipts as needed; monitor the credit extended to players; direct the preparation of summary sheets showing wager amounts and payouts; review operating expenses and budget estimates and wagering accounts and collection reports. Official definition text: Plan, direct, or coordinate gambling operations in a casino. May formulate house rules. The core of this occupation also includes familiarity with in-house games and marketing promotion, and managers exercise judgment within actual authorization; the task classification is not a uniform division of labor for everyone, and a cheating suspicion is not a criminal determination.
